Replace the whole content of paper/sections/s0_abstract.tex by:
Saturation-aware scheduling of direct velocity feedback (DVF) for active chatter damping picks, per spindle speed, the largest gain whose demand a proof-mass actuator can deliver. This paper analyses what the voltage clip does to the cut in a single-mode regenerative milling model. First, the published authority test, simulated with the step entry from rest that reproduces its gains, depends on the entry transient; an entry-independent condition bounds the steady forced command up to 0.9 of the stability limit, with a time-domain check of the clipped entry. Second, the forced orbit of the clipped loop has a bounded basin: a step entry (full engagement at $t=0$) chatters below 0.97 of the linear limit at 157 of 251 speeds, whereas a face entry reaches the limit, and at four speeds near the limit worst-phase kicks of 2.4--10.8\,\% of one tooth's cutting impulse cause chatter, against \SI{0.78}{\metre\per\second} or more without the clip at 16 points. Third, sector-condition linear matrix inequalities give ellipsoidal inner estimates of this basin, numerically verified on collocation models of the averaged and time-periodic dynamics; no simulated kick inside them caused chatter, and where the simulated basin is finite they are 1.5--28 times smaller than the critical kicks. The free voltage is small: 1.1--\SI{4.5}{\micro\metre} of runout uses up a \SI{10}{\percent} voltage margin. Finally, a published delayed term that vanishes on the forced orbit raises the linear limit by a median factor of 1.78 but the step-entry limit by only 1.03, and is fragile to loop delay with assumed second modes. The study is computational.

\section{Conclusions}\label{sec:conclusions}

Clipping the command of a velocity feedback loop at the force capacity of its proof-mass actuator changes the stability of a milling cut from a property of the linear system into a property of a basin. On the case study of \citet{ozsoy2026robust}, with a single-mode model that classifies 17 of its 19 published cutting tests as measured, the following was found.
\begin{enumerate}
\item With the step entry from rest that reproduces the published gains at high speeds, the authority test of saturation-aware gain scheduling is set by the entry transient. Bounding the steady forced demand in closed form at every depth up to $0.9\,\alim$, with a time-domain check of the clipped entry, gives an entry-independent gain map. With gains up to \SI{1500}{\volt\second\per\metre} the checked depth averages \SI{15.87}{\milli\metre}, but the gain sits at this chosen bound at 157 of 251 speeds, and a checked depth is not a safe depth: it lies inside the bistable band at 104 of the 109 speeds where the band was found.
\item The forced orbit of the clipped loop has a bounded basin, outside which the model ends in large-amplitude clipped chatter. A step entry from rest (full engagement at $t=0$) chatters below $0.97\,\alim$ at 157 of 251 speeds, whereas a face entry reaches at least $0.985\,\alim$ at every speed. At four speeds and $0.98\,\alim$, worst-phase velocity kicks of 2.4--10.8\,\% of one tooth's cutting impulse (3--\SI{13}{\micro\metre} of equivalent displacement) end the cut in chatter; without the clip, only kicks of \SI{0.78}{\metre\per\second} or more did so at the 16 points tested. At the linear limit the basin keeps a finite size, set by the voltage $\Vmax-\bmax$ that the forced command leaves free.
\item Sector-condition LMIs with a dead zone that moves with the forced command give ellipsoidal inner estimates of this basin, numerically verified on collocation models of the averaged and of the time-periodic milling model. No simulated kick inside them ended in chatter; where the simulated basin was finite they are 1.5 to 28 times smaller than the simulated critical kicks, mainly because of the certificate rather than of averaging. They cover instantaneous perturbations only.
\item The free voltage is small: for DVF designs that keep 10\,\% of the voltage free, 1.1--\SI{4.5}{\micro\metre} of eccentric runout brings the forced command to the clip.
\item A published delayed difference term that vanishes on the forced orbit raises the linear limit by a median factor of 1.78 ($g_2=\SI{2000}{\volt\second\per\metre}$) under the same authority rule, but the step-entry limit by only 1.03, and at the same forced command it widens the simulated basin by a median factor of 1.14. With assumed second modes at 400--\SI{800}{\hertz} it tolerates only about 100--\SI{200}{\micro\second} of loop delay, against \SI{300}{\micro\second} for DVF.
\end{enumerate}
All results are computational. Extending the certificates to the delay equation, assessing the free voltage against runout, edge forces and noise, and testing the bistability experimentally are the next steps.

edits.fix_old: To the authors' knowledge, no work has measured the basin of attraction of the stable cut, or certified a region of attraction around it, for a fixed active-damping law whose actuator saturates in milling. For a DVF law whose command is clipped at the actuator capacity in a regenerative milling model, this leaves open (i) how the authority condition of a saturation-aware gain map should be posed so that it is well defined, (ii) how far the clip exposes the linearly stable cut to chatter across the speed range, and how this depends on the way the tool enters the cut, (iii) how large a basin around the forced orbit can be guaranteed when part of the authority is spent on the forced vibration,
edits.fix_new: That the basin of the stable cut is bounded above the uncontrolled stability limit is expected: there the open-loop cut is exponentially unstable, and with a bounded input the null-controllable region of such a system is bounded along its unstable modes, so that no bounded feedback can stabilise it globally \citep{hu2001book}. To the authors' knowledge, however, the size of this basin has not been measured, nor a region of attraction around the stable cut certified, for a fixed active-damping law whose actuator saturates in milling. For a DVF law whose command is clipped at the actuator capacity in a regenerative milling model, this leaves open (i) how the authority condition of a saturation-aware gain map can be posed independently of the entry transient, (ii) how far the clip exposes the linearly stable cut to chatter across the speed range, and how this depends on the way the tool enters the cut, (iii) how large an inner estimate of the basin around the forced orbit can be certified when part of the authority is spent on the forced vibration,

edits.fix_new: \item Inner estimates of the basin (Section~\ref{sec:certificates}): ellipsoidal sets around the forced orbit from sector-condition LMIs. items.instruction: Add at the end of Section 5.6: 'For design, the averaged certificate C2 is the practical choice; C3 serves to show that averaging does not cause the gap, and its sizes are conservative in the number of segments.' Quote C3 at M = 32 where compared at 0.9 a_lim (c3_decomp.npz) and state that at 2500 rpm/0.98 a_lim the best candidates failed only the round-off bound.
